situation:
You are the operations manager for COPPER LARK JEWELRY, a handmade jewelry brand with four studios and the largest share of the regional market for hand-cut silver pieces. The owner (judge) started the company at a single bench sixteen years ago, has watched two national chains open nearby since, and intends to sell the company and retire in about three years.

Every piece is cut, soldered and finished by the eight bench artisans in the flagship studio. That is what customers are told, and it is what they pay a premium for. The coffee bar at the front of the flagship carries the same story, down to the design of its printed menu, and the brand's whole position in the region rests on it.

The company wants to open two stores in the next state, its first outside the region, and the overhead per piece will not support that. A contract workshop across the state line will cut and hand-finish the entry-level line for a third of what the same work costs at the benches. The brand's attorney has confirmed the pieces could still be sold and labelled as handmade.

That lower overhead would pay for both out-of-state stores and raise the price the business fetches when the owner (judge) sells. It would also take the entry-level line away from the eight bench artisans, and customers who pay a premium for pieces they believe are made at the flagship benches would object if they learned where the entry-level line now comes from.

Keeping every piece at the benches holds that story intact, but overhead stays where it is, the expansion shrinks to one store about two years later, and the sale price falls with it. The owner (judge) wants your recommendation and the measures that would show afterwards whether it was the right one. The owner (judge) will greet you, ask to hear your ideas, and will thank you after your presentation and questions.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the owner (judge) of COPPER LARK JEWELRY. Business background is the same as the situation above.

You started the company at one bench sixteen years ago and you intend to sell it and retire in about three years. You want to hear whether the operations manager would move the entry-level line to the contract workshop across the state line or keep every piece at the flagship benches, and what that choice does to overhead, to the expansion and to the price the business fetches.

During the presentation you will ask the following questions:
judgeQuestions: A year from now, how would we know this was the right call?
What would tell us early that it was not?
